results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and the data in the Statement.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice supplies the Countable and Dependent Choice hypotheses of the integration and approximation suppliers. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration]])

[F1] Gaussian kernels have unit mass, solve the heat equation, and have Gaussian spatial derivative bounds. They form an approximate identity, which converges in $L^2$; convolution obeys Young's inequality. ([[lem-heat-kernel-normalisation-scaling-and-derivatives]], [[lem-gaussian-kernels-form-an-approximate-identity]], [[thm-l-one-approximate-identities-converge-in-l-p]], [[thm-young-convolution-inequality]])

[F2] Dominated convergence and Holder's inequality apply to the displayed Lebesgue integrals. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]], [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]])



1.1 The square of $w_0$ near zero is $y^{-1}(\log(1/y))^{-2\alpha}$, integrable because $2\alpha>1$; its first power is also integrable. For $y,z>0$, $G_t(y-z)\ge G_t(y+z)$, proving positivity. Its integral in either positive variable is at most $1$. Thus the positive kernel is an $L^1$ contraction; Jensen's inequality in its subprobability measure, followed by integration in $y$, proves the $L^2$ contraction. Equivalently the latter follows by Young applied to the odd extension $\widetilde w_0$ on the line, whose heat evolution remains odd; restricting the equal two halfline norms gives the same bound. The Gaussian derivative bounds justify differentiating the convolution for every $t>0$, and give $w_t=\nu w_{yy}$ and the zero boundary value. Approximate-identity convergence applied to $\widetilde w_0$ gives strong $L^2$ initial convergence. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix a smooth $\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ equal to $0$ on $[0,1]$ and $1$ on $[2,\infty)$. The explicit $w_{0,j}(y)=\beta(jy)w_0(y)$ are smooth and compactly supported away from zero and converge to $w_0$ in $L^2$ by dominated convergence. Evolve their odd extensions. Integration by parts on the line, with Gaussian tails, gives $\|w(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|w_y\|_2^2=\|w_0\|_2^2$ for each approximant. Applying this identity to differences makes the evolutions Cauchy in $L^\infty_tL^2_y$ and their derivatives Cauchy in $L^2_{t,y}$. Their limit is the kernel evolution by its contraction, and its weak derivative is the derivative limit by integration against compactly supported tests. This gives the stated energy inequality. For a smooth halfline function vanishing at zero and decaying at infinity, the fundamental theorem gives $\|w\|_\infty^2\le2\|w\|_2\|w_y\|_2$, hence $\|w\|_4^4\le2\|w\|_2^3\|w_y\|_2$. Time integration, the energy bound and Holder prove the $L^4$ assertion; approximation passes the inequality to this $w$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 Integrating the Gaussian kernel first in $y$ gives $M(t)=\int_0^\infty\operatorname{erf}(z/(2\sqrt{\nu t}))w_0(z)\,dz$, where $\operatorname{erf}(r)=2\pi^{-1/2}\int_0^r e^{-s^2}\,ds$. Dominated convergence gives $M(t)\to M_0$, and differentiation for positive time gives $$m'(t)=-\frac{t^{-3/2}}{2\sqrt{\pi\nu}}\int_0^\infty z e^{-z^2/(4\nu t)}w_0(z)\,dz.$$ After $z=\sqrt t\,r$, the prefactor is $t^{-3/4}$. The integral on $1\le r\le2$ is bounded below by $cL(t)^{-\alpha}$ for small $t$. For $r\le t^{-1/4}$, $\log(1/(\sqrt t r))\ge L(t)/4$, so the integral is bounded above by $CL(t)^{-\alpha}\int_0^\infty r^{1/2}e^{-r^2/(4\nu)}\,dr$. For $r>t^{-1/4}$ the Gaussian tail is exponentially small; on the support of $\eta(\sqrt t r)$ the logarithmic factor is uniformly bounded above, which gives the same upper bound. This proves both derivative bounds. Integrating the upper bound from zero gives $|m(t)|\le Ct^{1/4}L(t)^{-\alpha}$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The upper derivative bound is integrable. The lower bound gives $\int_0^{t_*}|m'|^{4/3}\ge c\int_0^{t_*}t^{-1}L(t)^{-4\alpha/3}\,dt=\infty$, since $4\alpha/3\le1$. In contrast the squared critical-corrector expression is at most $Ct^{-1}L(t)^{-2\alpha}$, which is integrable since $2\alpha>1$. Away from time zero every quantity is smooth, proving all stated time-integral conclusions. [step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Differentiating the tail integral gives $h_y=w$ and $h_t=\nu w_y=\nu h_{yy}$; the boundary term at infinity vanishes by Gaussian decay. Also $h(t,y)=\int_0^yw(t,z)\,dz-M(t)$. Thus on $[0,B]$ its difference from $h_0$ is at most $\sqrt B\|w(t)-w_0\|_2+|M(t)-M_0|$, which tends to zero. Finally a positive separation between $y$ and $\operatorname{supp}w_0$ puts every differentiated Gaussian convolution under the bound $C_Nt^{-N}e^{-c/t}\|w_0\|_1$. These arguments prove the remaining assertions. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, the square, smooth $b,\rho$, and the parameters of the Statement.

[F1] The product and chain rules apply to these finite products of smooth scalar functions. ([[thm-chain-sum-product-and-composition-rules-for-banach-derivatives]])

[F2] A function supported in a set of area at most $A$ and bounded by $B$ has $L^2$ norm at most $A^{1/2}B$. ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]])



1.1 The product formula shows that $R_\ell=1$ whenever some $d_i<\ell/3$, and $R_\ell=0$ whenever every $d_i\ge\ell$. The supporting union has area at most $4\ell$. Smoothness follows from the finite product. Because $b=0$ on each side, the fundamental theorem in its normal coordinate gives $|b(x,y)|\le C d_i(x,y)$ for every side $i$, and $\nabla b$ and all fixed higher derivatives are bounded on the closed square. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Expand $D^k(bR_\ell)$ by the product rule. Every spatial derivative on a cutoff costs at most $C\ell^{-1}$. If at least one cutoff is differentiated, choose that side $i$; on that term's support $d_i\le\ell$, so an undifferentiated $b$ supplies a factor $C\ell$. Thus the terms with no derivative on $b$ have magnitude at most $C\ell^{1-k}$. If $j\ge1$ derivatives hit $b$, the other factors cost at most $C\ell^{-(k-j)}\le C\ell^{1-k}$. Terms with no differentiated cutoff have the same bound for $k\ge1$. All terms are supported in the union from step 1.1. Therefore $\|D^k(bR_\ell)\|_2\le C\ell^{3/2-k}$ for $k=1,2,3$; for $k=1$ the pointwise bound also gives $\|\nabla(bR_\ell)\|_\infty\le C$. Intersections of strips require no disjointness: the bound uses any differentiated side and the total union area. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 With $\ell=\sqrt t$, a time derivative of $\rho(d_i/\ell)$ is bounded by $Ct^{-1}$ and is supported where $d_i\le\ell$. One extra spatial derivative costs at most $C\ell^{-1}$, offset by $b=O(\ell)$ if it does not hit $b$. If it hits $b$, its derivative is bounded. Hence $|\partial_t\nabla(bR_{\sqrt t})|\le Ct^{-1}$ on the same union of strips, and its $L^2$ norm is at most $Ct^{-1}\ell^{1/2}$. Differentiating $r$ and applying step 2.1 with $k=1,2,3$ gives every asserted bound for $r$, $r_t$ and $\Delta r$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Near each boundary point $R_\ell=1$, so the boundary value of $bR_\ell$ is zero and its normal derivative equals that of $b$. Subtraction therefore cancels the stated stream trace and normal derivative. The tangential derivative of a zero boundary stream is zero, so its rotation has both zero normal and zero tangential velocity on each side. For $x\in J$ and sufficiently small $t$, the cutoffs of the vertical sides vanish identically and $R$ depends only on $y$. Since $b(x,0)=b(x,1)=0$, also $b_x,b_{xx}$ vanish on those edges and satisfy $|b_x|+|b_{xx}|\le C\min(y,1-y)$. Consequently $\partial_xr=-m\operatorname{rot}(b_xR)$ is bounded by $C_J|m|$: the only factor $R_y=O(\ell^{-1})$ is multiplied by $b_x=O(\ell)$ in its supporting strip. This proves the last estimate and completes the proof. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Countable Choice, the domain, mesh, spaces, face-average interpolant and existing Fortin map in the Statement.

[A1] Countable Choice is inherited from the face-average interpolant and Fortin construction. No point evaluations or additional choice principle are used. ([[def-countable-choice]], [[lem-na-scott-zhang-boundary-preserving-p1-interpolant]], [[thm-na-mini-element-fortin-stability]])

[F1] The face-average interpolant is defined on $H^1(D)$, reproduces global affine polynomials, and satisfies $\|w-I_hw\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Its proof step 2.1 establishes that for $v\in H^2(D)$ there is an affine polynomial $p$ on each patch with $\|v-p\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}\le Ch_K^2\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ and $\|\nabla(v-p)\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. It also gives $\|\nabla(v-I_hv)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$, uniformly bounded patch overlap and comparable cell diameters within each patch. ([[lem-na-scott-zhang-boundary-preserving-p1-interpolant]])

[F2] The existing Fortin construction has the formula in the Statement, maps $H^1_0(D)^d$ into $V_h$, and preserves $b(\Pi_hv,q_h)=b(v,q_h)$ for every $q_h\in Q_h$. ([[thm-na-mini-element-fortin-stability]])

[F3] MINI bubble scaling gives $\int_Kb_K\ge c|K|$, $\|b_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le C|K|^{1/2}$, and $\|\nabla b_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K^{-1}|K|^{1/2}$. ([[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]], [[lem-shape-regular-affine-simplex-scaling]])

[F4] The spaces satisfy $V_\sigma=\{v\in H^1_0(D)^d:b(v,q)=0\text{ for all }q\in L^2_0(D)\}$ and $Z_h=\{v_h\in V_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\text{ for all }q_h\in Q_h\}$. The finite-dimensional kernel $Z_h$ is closed in Hilbert $L^2(D)^d$; its orthogonal projection is the unique best $L^2$ approximation and agrees on $V_h$ with the mass projector of the discrete Helmholtz theorem. ([[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]], [[def-na-discrete-weak-and-exact-divergence-free-spaces]], [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]], [[thm-na-discrete-helmholtz-projection-and-pressure-schur]])

[F5] Holder's inequality gives $|\int_Ke|\le |K|^{1/2}\|e\|_{L^2(K)}$ for vector-valued $e$, by Euclidean duality and the scalar inequality. ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]])



**Given:** The inputs and the same operators $I_h,\Pi_h$ specified in the Statement.

1.1 Fix a cell $K$ and first take one scalar component of $v$. Let $p$ be the affine patch approximant from [F1], regarded as a global affine polynomial on $D$. This causes no boundary restriction, because $I_h$ is defined on all of $H^1(D)$. Set $w=v-p$. Affine reproduction gives $v-I_hv=w-I_hw$ on $K$. Apply the first-order local $L^2$ estimate in [F1] to $w$ and its patch gradient estimate to obtain $\|v-I_hv\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|\nabla(v-p)\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}\le Ch_K^2\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Apply this componentwise and sum squares for vector $v$. The local gradient bound $\|\nabla(v-I_hv)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ is also [F1]. All these estimates use facet averages and require no representative with point values. [A1, F1, given, choose]

1.2 Write $e_K=v-I_hv$ on $K$. The actual numerator of the Fortin coefficient is the unweighted integral of $e_K$, so [F3] and [F5] give $|c_K|\le |K|^{1/2}(\int_Kb_K)^{-1}\|e_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le C|K|^{-1/2}\|e_K\|_{L^2(K)}$. Hence $\|b_Kc_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le C\|e_K\|_{L^2(K)}$ and $\|\nabla(b_Kc_K)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K^{-1}\|e_K\|_{L^2(K)}$. No bound involving a global inverse mesh scale is used. [F2, F3, F5, algebra]

2.1 Bubble interiors are disjoint, so on $K$ the existing map satisfies $v-\Pi_hv=e_K-b_Kc_K$. The triangle inequality, step 1.2 and step 1.1 imply $\|v-\Pi_hv\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K^2\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ and $\|\nabla(v-\Pi_hv)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. The zero-boundary membership of $\Pi_hv$ is already ensured by [F2]. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Square and sum the two estimates in step 2.1. Since $h_K\le h$ and the patch overlap is uniformly bounded by [F1], $\sum_Kh_K^4\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}^2\le Ch^4\|D^2v\|_2^2$ and $\sum_Kh_K^2\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}^2\le Ch^2\|D^2v\|_2^2$. Taking square roots proves the two global approximation estimates, with the asserted dependence of constants. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Suppose $v\in H^2(D)^d\cap V_\sigma$. Because $Q_h\subset L^2_0(D)$, [F4] gives $b(v,q_h)=0$ for every $q_h\in Q_h$. Fortin preservation [F2] therefore puts $\Pi_hv\in Z_h$. Best approximation [F4] and step 3.1 give $\|(I-P_{Z_h})v\|_2\le\|v-\Pi_hv\|_2\le Ch^2\|D^2v\|_2$. This uses only $L^2$ orthogonality, with no $H^1$ estimate for $P_{Z_h}$. [F2, F4, step 3.1, given]

5.1 Finally let $X=H^2(D)^d\cap V_\sigma$ with its $H^2$ norm and suppose $u\in W^{1,\infty}(0,T;X)$. By this Bochner Sobolev hypothesis, $u(t)$ and $u_t(t)$ belong to $X$ for almost every $t$, and their $H^2$ norms have the stated essential bounds. Apply step 4.1 separately to these two fields at such times and take essential suprema. The two claimed time-dependent estimates follow. Together with steps 2.1 and 3.1 this proves every assertion. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, given] ∎

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, a viscosity $\nu>0$, the square $D$, and the following explicit choices and conventions. Write $\operatorname{rot}\psi=(\psi_y,-\psi_x)$. Choose nonzero $a\in C_c^\infty((1/3,2/3))$, $1/2<\alpha\le3/4$, and the functions $w_0,w,h,M_0,m$ of [[lem-na-halfline-heat-logarithmic-mass-loss]]. Choose smooth $\kappa,\chi$ equal to $1$ on $[0,1/8]$ and $0$ on $[1/4,1]$. All time bounds below are on a sufficiently small $T>0$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice supplies the choice hypotheses of the integration, Hilbert-space and evolution interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration]])

[F1] The halfline construction supplies $w_t=\nu w_{yy}$, $h_y=w$, $h_t=\nu h_{yy}$, $h(t,0)=-M_0-m(t)$, $w(t,0)=0$, $\sup_t\|w\|_{L^1\cap L^2}<\infty$, $w_y\in L^2_{t,y}$, $w\in L^4_{t,y}$, strong initial $L^2$ convergence, local uniform initial convergence of $h$, and the logarithmic estimates on $m,m'$. ([[lem-na-halfline-heat-logarithmic-mass-loss]])

[F2] On the square the explicit $R_{\sqrt t}$ correction for a smooth boundary-zero $b$ has the trace cancellation, spatial estimates, time estimates and interior tangential derivative estimate stated in [[lem-na-shrinking-boundary-stream-corrector]].

[F3] The solenoidal class uses $V_\sigma=\{v\in H^1_0(D)^2:\operatorname{div}v=0\}$, $H_\sigma=\overline{V_\sigma}^{L^2}$ and $Q=L^2_0(D)$. The skew convection agrees with $(u\cdot\nabla)u$ for a divergence-free zero-boundary velocity. The weak Newtonian viscous term agrees with $\nu(\nabla u,\nabla v)$ for such a velocity, by integration by parts and $\operatorname{div}u=0$. ([[def-na-solenoidal-energy-weak-ns-velocity]], [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]], [[def-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form]], [[lem-na-zero-mean-of-zero-boundary-divergence]])

[F4] The bounded divergence right inverse recovers a unique mean-zero $L^2$ pressure from its full-test divergence pairing. ([[thm-na-bounded-lipschitz-domain-divergence-right-inverse]])

[F5] The MINI convergence theorem supplies solenoidal energy weak subsequential velocities for the stated data. ([[thm-na-mini-navier-stokes-be-subsequential-limit]])

[F6] Holder and dominated convergence are available. ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]])

[F7] Two-dimensional solenoidal energy velocities with these data are unique, with the strong trace and restricted-derivative facts proved in [[lem-na-two-dimensional-solenoidal-energy-velocity-uniqueness]].

[F8] In one dimension there is a smooth $[0,1]$-valued bump equal to $1$ on $[-r,r]$ and supported in $(-R,R)$ for every $0<r<R$. Translation, restriction and finite products give interval cutoffs. ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]])



1.1 The choices in **Given** exist by [F8]: take a bump centered at $1/2$ with inner radius $1/24$ and outer radius $1/12$ for $a$, giving a nonzero function compactly supported in $(1/3,2/3)$. Restrict zero-centered bumps to the positive halfline with radii $(1/32,1/16)$ for $\eta$, $(1/8,1/4)$ for $\kappa$ and $\chi$, and $(1/3,1)$ for $\rho$. They have every stated support, plateau and sign property. Put $a_n=2\int_0^1a(x)\sin(n\pi x)\,dx$ and define $$\theta(x,y)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n\sin(n\pi x)\frac{\sinh(n\pi(1-y))}{\sinh(n\pi)},\qquad \widetilde\phi(x,y)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n\cos(n\pi x)\frac{\cosh(n\pi(1-y))}{\sinh(n\pi)}.$$ Repeated integration by parts makes $|a_n|\le C_Nn^{-N}$ for every $N$, since $a$ vanishes near the endpoints. The hyperbolic factors and their derivatives of order $k$ are bounded by $C_kn^k$ uniformly on $[0,1]$. Thus every differentiated series converges absolutely uniformly, and both functions are smooth on the closed square and harmonic. The sine series equals $a$ at $y=0$: indeed the odd, $2$-periodic smooth extension of $a$ has its Fourier series equal to itself. To verify this last assertion directly, its rapid coefficients define a uniformly convergent Fourier series with the same coefficients; their difference has all Fourier coefficients zero. Convolution with the Fejer kernels, which are nonnegative unit-mass kernels concentrating at zero by their formula $N^{-1}|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{ij\pi x}|^2$, converges uniformly to a continuous periodic function by uniform continuity; it vanishes for a function whose coefficients all vanish. Hence the difference is zero. The other boundary values of $\theta$ are zero. Direct differentiation gives $\widetilde\phi_x=\theta_y$ and $\widetilde\phi_y=-\theta_x$. Let $\phi=\widetilde\phi-\int_D\widetilde\phi$, so $\phi\in Q$, $\nabla\phi=\operatorname{rot}\theta$, and $\|\phi\|_2>0$ because $a\ne0$ makes $\theta$ nonconstant. [A1, F8, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Define $b=\theta-a\chi$. This is smooth and zero on all four sides. Its normal derivative equals $\partial_n\theta$ everywhere on the boundary: at the bottom $\chi'=0$, at the top $\chi=\chi'=0$, and near the vertical sides $a=a'=0$. Take the function $R(t)=R_{\sqrt t}$ from [F2] and choose $T$ small enough for that construction, with $\sqrt T<1/16$. Set $$\psi_m=a(x)[\kappa(y)h(t,y)+M_0\chi(y)],\qquad \psi=\psi_m+m(t)\theta-m(t)bR(t),$$ $$u=\operatorname{rot}\psi,\qquad p=-m'(t)\phi,\qquad r=-m(t)\operatorname{rot}(bR(t)).$$ All these fields are smooth for $t>0$. On the bottom $\psi_m=-am$, $\theta=a$, and $b=0$; on the other sides $\psi_m=\theta=b=0$. Thus $\psi=0$ on the boundary. The normal derivative of $\psi_m$ is zero on every side: on the bottom it is, up to its sign, $a w(t,0)=0$, and on all other sides the fixed cutoffs or $a,a'$ vanish. Hence $\partial_n(\psi_m+m\theta)=m\partial_n b$, and [F2] makes $\partial_n\psi=0$. Thus $u(t)\in V_\sigma$ exactly, with no-slip on every edge including compatible corner values. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Write $L(t)=\log(1/t)$. By [F1] and [F2], $$\|r\|_\infty\le C|m|,\quad \|r\|_2\le C|m|t^{1/4},\quad \|\nabla r\|_2\le C|m|t^{-1/4},$$ $$\|r_t\|_2+\|\Delta r\|_2\le C(|m'|t^{1/4}+|m|t^{-3/4})\le Ct^{-1/2}L(t)^{-\alpha}.$$ The last function is square integrable near zero because $2\alpha>1$. In particular $r\in L^\infty_tL^2_x\cap L^2_tH^1_x$ and $r(t)\to0$ strongly in $L^2$. The main stream rotation has a uniform $L^2$ bound from bounded $h$ and bounded $\|w\|_2$. Its gradient uses only bounded $h$, $w$ with fixed coefficients and $w_y$ with fixed coefficients, so the heat energy bound makes it $L^2_{t,x}$. The smooth field $m\operatorname{rot}\theta$ has the same required bounds. We obtain $$u\in L^\infty(0,T;L^2(D)^2)\cap L^2(0,T;V_\sigma).$$ [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The outer harmonic field cancels the entire rough gradient: $(\partial_t-\nu\Delta)(m\operatorname{rot}\theta)+\nabla p=m'\nabla\phi-m'\nabla\phi=0$. The main stream has the explicit residual $$(\partial_t-\nu\Delta)\psi_m=-\nu[a''\kappa h+2a\kappa'w+a\kappa''h]-\nu M_0[a''\chi+a\chi''].$$ Its rotation contains only fixed coefficients times $h,w$, except for terms with $\kappa'w_y$. The latter are supported in $y\ge1/8$, a fixed positive distance from $\operatorname{supp}w_0\subset[0,1/16]$, and are square integrable by the off-support Gaussian bound in [F1]. All other terms are uniformly $L^2$ bounded. Together with step 3.1 this proves $$F_L=(\partial_t-\nu\Delta)u+\nabla p\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^2).$$ [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 Let $h_0(y)=-\int_y^\infty w_0(z)\,dz$, $\psi_0=a[\kappa h_0+M_0\chi]$, and $u_0=\operatorname{rot}\psi_0$. Strong $L^2$ convergence of $w$, uniform convergence of $h$ on $[0,1]$, $m(t)\to0$ and step 3.1 give $u(t)\to u_0$ strongly in $L^2$. The stream $\psi_0$ is $H^1$, supported away from the other three sides, and vanishes on the bottom because $h_0(0)=-M_0$. Here is a direct approximation proving $\psi_0\in H^1_0$, without relying on an unstated trace theorem. Near the bottom it equals $a(x)\int_0^yw_0(z)\,dz$. If a cutoff removes $0<y<\varepsilon$, the derivative-of-cutoff error is bounded in squared $L^2$ by $$C\varepsilon^{-2}\int_0^{2\varepsilon}\left|\int_0^yw_0(z)\,dz\right|^2dy\le C\int_0^{2\varepsilon}|w_0(z)|^2\,dz\longrightarrow0.$$ The inequality follows from $|\int_0^y w_0|^2\le y\int_0^y|w_0|^2$ and integrating $y\le2\varepsilon$. The other errors tend to zero by absolute continuity of the integrals of $|\psi_0|^2+|\nabla\psi_0|^2$. The cut-off streams are smooth and compactly supported inside $D$, since $w_0$ is smooth away from zero. Their rotations belong to $V_\sigma$ and converge to $u_0$ in $L^2$, proving $u_0\in H_\sigma$ by its actual closure definition. [F1, F3, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 The normal component $u_2$ is uniformly bounded in space and time: $-\partial_x\psi_m$ uses only bounded $h$ and fixed functions, the harmonic term has bounded amplitude $m$, and $r$ is uniformly bounded. Thus $u_2\partial_yu\in L^2_{t,x}$ by step 3.1. The only unbounded part of $u_1$ is $a\kappa w$. Choose $J\Subset(0,1)$ containing $\operatorname{supp}a$ and decrease $T$ so the last estimate in [F2] applies there. On $J\times(0,1)$, $\partial_xr$ is uniformly bounded; the main and harmonic terms satisfy $|\partial_xu|\le C(1+|w|)$, so $|u_1\partial_xu|\le C(1+|w|^2)$. This belongs to $L^2_{t,x}$ by $w\in L^4_{t,y}$. Outside $J$, the coefficient $a$ vanishes and $u_1$ is bounded, so $u_1\partial_xu\in L^2_{t,x}$ there by the energy-gradient bound. Hence $N(u)=(u\cdot\nabla)u\in L^2_{t,x}$. Define $f=F_L+N(u)$. It belongs to $L^2_tL^2_x$, and the pointwise positive-time equation is $u_t-\nu\Delta u+N(u)+\nabla p=f$. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 On $[\varepsilon,T]$, integrate the smooth equation from step 5.1 against $u$. The convection and pressure integrals vanish by divergence and no slip. Thus $$\tfrac12\|u(t)\|_2^2+\nu\int_\varepsilon^t\|\nabla u\|_2^2=\tfrac12\|u(\varepsilon)\|_2^2+\int_\varepsilon^t(f,u).$$ Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$: strong initial convergence handles the endpoint and the energy and force bounds handle both integrals. This gives energy equality with initial value $u_0$. Similarly integrate the positive-time equation against a fixed solenoidal $V$ test and a smooth scalar time test, integrate by parts in time, and send $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The pressure term vanishes; all remaining integrals converge by the established bounds. The resulting identity is precisely the solenoidal weak equation with initial value $u_0$. Positive-time smoothness and strong initial convergence give the required weak continuity on $[0,T]$. Thus $u$ is a solenoidal energy weak velocity of [F3]. [F3, F6, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 4.2, algebra]

6.2 The pressure has zero spatial mean and is in $L^1_tQ$, since $m'\in L^1$ and $\phi\in Q$. It defines a time-distribution pressure for the full momentum equation: test the pointwise equation on compact positive-time intervals; its time-distribution identity on $(0,T)$ follows directly. Also $\|p(t)\|_2=|m'(t)|\|\phi\|_2$, so [F1] and $\|\phi\|_2>0$ imply $p\notin L^{4/3}_tQ$. If a second mean-zero $Q$-valued pressure distribution $q$ represented this same velocity and force, subtract their momentum equations. For each scalar time test $\zeta$, the $Q$ element $\langle q-p,\zeta\rangle$ has zero divergence pairing with every $V$ test. Pair with the bounded divergence right inverse of that very element, using [F4], to show its squared norm is zero. Thus $q=p$ as $Q$-valued distributions. In particular, if $q\in L^{4/3}_tQ$, both are $L^1_tQ$ functions and equality of their distributions gives equality almost everywhere (test against a countable dense set in $Q$ and scalar tests), contradicting the nonintegrability just proved. Consequently this velocity does not meet the regular-pressure definition named in the Counterexample. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 By [[lem-na-two-dimensional-solenoidal-energy-velocity-uniqueness]], the constructed solenoidal energy velocity is the unique one for these two-dimensional square data. Every actual MINI subsequential limit supplied by [F5] is a solenoidal energy weak velocity with these same data, hence equals $u$. Steps 1.1–5.1 give all concrete properties and show that no mean-zero endpoint-integrable pressure exists for that limit. This refutes the universal regular-pressure assertion. [F5, step 6.1, step 6.2, F7, algebra] ∎
